Flow matching generates stochastic trajectories. It starts from random noise
and gradually transforms it into an output conditioned on the simulator inputs.
Use it when the variability between simulations matters, not just their average.

It supports static inputs and full observed sequences. With sequence conditioning,
it uses the whole supplied path; this is conditional generation rather than a
causal forecast.

## Try it

This small continuous-valued example uses 40 parameter settings, four
realisations per setting and eight time points. The response is
$y(t)=\theta(1+\sin t)+0.3\cos t+\epsilon$, with independent
$\epsilon\sim N(0,0.08^2)$. The known mean lets us see what the surrogate learns.
This is a short teaching fit, not a benchmark of the model families.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Create the example bank"
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from metis import SimulationDataset, Surrogate, TrainingConfig

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
times = np.linspace(0, 2, 8)
inputs = np.repeat(np.linspace(0.2, 1.2, 40)[:, None], 4, axis=0)
mean = inputs[:, None, :] * (1 + np.sin(times)[None, :, None])
mean = mean + 0.3 * np.cos(times)[None, :, None]
outputs = mean + rng.normal(0, 0.08, mean.shape)
bank = SimulationDataset.from_arrays(
    inputs, outputs, input_names=["theta"], output_names=["response"], times=times,
)
split = bank.split(seed=42)
```

```{python}
model = Surrogate(
    "flow_matching",
    model_options={"n_blocks": 1, "n_head": 2, "n_kv_head": 2, "embd_dim": 32},
).fit(
    split.train, split.validation,
    config=TrainingConfig(steps=300, batch_size=32, eval_every=50, seed=42),
)
```

Generate 100 trajectories at one held-out parameter setting. The shaded band
shows pointwise 5th–95th percentiles of these draws; it represents the fitted
model's variability, not uncertainty in its fitted weights.

```{python}
theta = split.test.inputs[:1]
draws = model.sample(theta, n_samples=100, seed=13, num_steps=30, solver="heun")[0, :, :, 0]
expected = theta[0, 0] * (1 + np.sin(times)) + 0.3 * np.cos(times)
print("Draws × time points:", draws.shape)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot generated trajectories"
#| fig-cap: "Flow matching: short CPU fit on the synthetic continuous bank. The shaded band contains the middle 90% of surrogate draws at each time."
low, high = np.quantile(draws, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.fill_between(times, low, high, alpha=0.25, label="Surrogate 90% band")
ax.plot(times, draws[:8].T, color="C0", alpha=0.15, linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(times, draws.mean(axis=0), color="C0", label="Surrogate sample mean")
ax.plot(times, expected, "--", color="black", label="Known mean")
ax.plot(times, split.test.outputs[0, :, 0], "o", color="C1", label="Held-out realisation")
ax.set(xlabel="Time", ylabel="Response")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For a real bank, assess coverage over many held-out settings using the
[evaluation tools](../package/evaluation.qmd).

## How it works
The flow matching surrogate is parametrised with a *non-causal* transformer that processes the entire sequence in parallel.

### Flow Matching

Flow matching models learn time-varying velocity fields which can be used to transport a sample of pure noise (e.g. from a Gaussian) to the data distribution. In order to generate samples the time-varying velocity field $v_{\theta}$ must be integrated over time $t$ to transport a noise sample $x_0$ to the data distribution:
$$
x_{\mathrm{pred}} = x_0+\int_{t=0}^{t=1}v_{\theta}(x_t|c)dt\text{, where } c \text{ is conditioning (i.e. surrogate inputs)}
$$


In practice this is achieved via numerical ODE solvers like Euler or Heun, with the number of solver steps introducing a trade-off between speed and quality.

:::{.callout-note  title="Technical note" collapse="true"}
Diffusion models have equivalent ODE and SDE forms and can be sampled via SDE-solvers like Euler-Maruyama or ODE-solvers like Heun. See @song2021scorebased.
:::

By fixing the conditioning $c$ and varying the initial noise, you can sample multiple realisations rather than the average realisation that an MLP or Autoregressive transformer learn.

For more background, see the [introduction to normalising flows and flow matching](https://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/blog/2024/01/20/flow-matching.html).

## Training and sampling settings

`n_blocks` controls depth and `embd_dim` controls width. The default has two
blocks, width 64 and four query/key-value heads.

```bash
uv run metis train model=flow_matching model.model_options.embd_dim=128 evaluation.num_steps=100
```

`interpolant` chooses a linear (`linear`, default) or trigonometric (`trig`)
noise-to-data training path. Sampling has separate settings: `num_steps` controls
integration effort, and `solver` chooses Euler or Heun. More solver steps cost
more time; compare predictions to determine whether they help.
